items.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024
items.q: we’re also telling these young guys before you go to Brad you have to check out Wynton, because Brad checked out Wynton.

ctx.x: He said this about American jazz. He says — he was talking about playing with visiting jazz musicians. “It’s an honor because jazz to me has always been, historically speaking, a pure American art form that’s so powerful, so joyful that it spread throughout the world.” And another quote from the pianist Rossano Sportiello from Italy, who now lives here. He said, “The most beautiful compliment that we could tell each other was, ‘Tonight you sounded like an American’.” So my question is nowadays do jazz musicians…

I think it’s more the latter than the former. You know I don’t know exactly like, the time period-wise, like when the university, the conservatory system started here with jazz departments, like I think maybe earlier in the States than it has over here. But like the main conservatory here in Paris, there are a lot of great young musicians and they’re definitely into, I don’t want to say avante garde, because it’s not just that, but it’s more about writing their own original music that has kind of like an ECM kind…
Glasper. You know so there’s more of that going on. So maybe influence by American musicians but a different generation of them.
